issues.legal_issue: A court reopening a decree in a statutory borrower-relief proceeding cannot investigate whether the decree-holder of record was a benamidar for another person.
material_facts: Applications sought reopening of money decrees under the Bengal Money-Lenders Act and alleged that the recorded decree-holders were benamidars for the person who had actually advanced the money.
The courts below investigated that allegation and treated the alleged real lender as the decree-holder for the purposes of relief.
issues.conclusion: The court was not competent in a proceeding under section 36 to go behind the decree and investigate whether the decree-holder on record was a benamidar; it had to treat the recorded decree-holders as the decree-holders.
issues.legal_principle: Section 36(1)(a) and section 36(2)(a)–(e) permit reopening a decree to provide the borrower the statutory relief, including recalculating the debt and adjusting the parties’ rights as specified in those provisions. Reopening does not erase the original adjudication or revive the original cause of action; the new decree is made in favour of the original decree-holder. The court relied on Renula v. Manmatha, 72 I.A. 156, and Bank of Commerce Ltd. v. Amulya Krishna Babu Roy Chowdhury, [1944] F.C.R. 126.

predicates.statutory_borrower_relief_reopening: The proceeding seeks statutory borrower relief by reopening an existing decree.
predicates.recorded_decreeholder_alleged_to_be_anot: A party alleges that the person named as decree-holder was acting as another person’s nominee in respect of the decree.

issues.definition: When a statutory borrower-relief proceeding reopens a decree and the recorded decree-holder is alleged to be another person’s nominee, the court must treat the recorded decree-holder as the decree-holder.

issues.legal_issue: In a statutory decree-reopening proceeding, the court may investigate whether an execution-sale purchaser or a person claiming through that purchaser acquired rights bona fide.
material_facts: The judgment-debtors sought restoration of properties sold in execution of the decrees.
Some properties had been purchased by the decree-holders and later transferred to another person; the courts found that the transfer was fictitious.
Another property had been bought at the execution sale by a person other than the decree-holders, who claimed it as her own purchase.
issues.conclusion: The court may inquire whether an ostensible purchaser at an execution sale, or a person claiming through a decree-holder purchaser, bona fide acquired rights; such an inquiry is within the provisions governing the protection of purchasers and restoration of property.
issues.legal_principle: Section 36(2)(b) protects qualifying bona fide acquisitions by persons other than the decree-holder, while section 36(2)(c) provides for restoration where the decree-holder purchased the property and the statutory conditions for restoration are met. Applying those provisions requires an inquiry into the bona fides of an ostensible purchaser or transferee, but does not permit an inquiry into whether the decree-holder of record was a benamidar.

predicates.statutory_borrower_relief_reopening: The proceeding seeks statutory borrower relief by reopening an existing decree.
predicates.execution_sale_purchaser_or_transferee_c: A person who bought property at an execution sale, or claims through such a purchaser, asserts rights in the property.

issues.definition: In a statutory decree-reopening proceeding, when an execution-sale purchaser or someone claiming through that purchaser asserts property rights, the court may inquire whether those rights were acquired bona fide.

issues.legal_issue: Property bought in execution by the decree-holder and transferred through a fictitious transaction to a person who did not bona fide acquire rights may be restored to the judgment-debtor.
material_facts: The decree-holders purchased two groups of properties at execution sales, with the sale proceeds set off against the decretal dues.
The decree-holders later executed a conveyance of those properties to another person, and the courts found that conveyance fictitious.
The judgment-debtors sought restoration of the properties in the proceedings to reopen the decrees.
issues.conclusion: The orders restoring those properties to the judgment-debtors were upheld because the decree-holders were the purchasers and the purported transferee had not bona fide acquired rights.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 36(2)(c) of the Bengal Money-Lenders Act, property sold in execution may be restored where the decree-holder purchased it and the statutory conditions apply. A person who did not bona fide acquire rights through a subsequent fictitious transfer does not obtain the protection contemplated by section 36(2)(b).

predicates.statutory_borrower_relief_reopening: The proceeding seeks statutory borrower relief by reopening an existing decree.
predicates.decreeholder_bought_property_at_executio: The decree-holder purchased the property at the execution sale.
predicates.subsequent_transferee_did_not_bona_fide_: A later transferee did not genuinely and bona fide acquire rights in the property.

issues.definition: When a decree is reopened in a statutory borrower-relief proceeding, the decree-holder bought the property at execution, and a later transferee did not bona fide acquire rights, the property must be restored to the judgment-debtor.

issues.legal_issue: A property bought at an execution sale by someone other than the decree-holder is not restored merely because the purchase money came from another person, where the decree-holder neither bought nor possessed the property.
material_facts: A property was purchased at the execution sale by a person other than the decree-holders.
The purchase money may have come from that purchaser’s husband, but the decree-holders did not buy the property.
There was no proof that the decree-holders possessed the property either directly or through the purchaser.
issues.conclusion: The property was not subject to restoration, and its possession remained with the execution-sale purchaser; the source of the purchase money was immaterial.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 36(2)(c) of the Bengal Money-Lenders Act, restoration on the basis that the decree-holder purchased property in execution does not apply when the decree-holder did not purchase it. The source of funds used by the person who purchased it does not alter that result where the decree-holder is not shown to have possessed the property directly or through that person.

predicates.statutory_borrower_relief_reopening: The proceeding seeks statutory borrower relief by reopening an existing decree.
predicates.another_person_bought_property_at_execut: A person other than the decree-holder purchased the property at the execution sale.
predicates.decreeholder_did_not_buy_property: The decree-holder was not the purchaser of the property at the execution sale.
predicates.decreeholder_not_shown_to_possess_proper: There is no proof that the decree-holder possessed the property directly or through the execution-sale purchaser.

issues.definition: When a statutory decree-reopening proceeding concerns property bought at execution by someone other than the decree-holder, and the decree-holder neither bought nor is shown to have possessed it, the property must not be restored to the judgment-debtor.
